# Plan: Multi-tenant Auth Refactor

## Context supplied by the plan author
The goal is to reorganize existing tenant-auth orchestration without changing
its product behavior. RequestPolicy groups the existing per-request access
decision: given already-fetched claims and tenant/request context, it returns
allow or deny under the existing access policy. AuthBroker.validateAndDispatch()
calls it after validation and before dispatch. It adds no policy, network call,
cache mutation or state. Its separate class boundary remains a proposal to review.

## Existing contracts retained
The existing cache adapter keys entries by tenant ID, issuer, audience,
and policy version. It evicts expired tokens and invalidates entries on
logout, token revocation, or tenant suspension. AuthCache retains these
unchanged validity and tenant-key rules; they do not serialize mutations.
AuthCache is a service-facing facade over that same existing adapter,
with one backing cache. The adapter, its invalidation hooks, and their
existing tests remain in use unchanged.
Unit and integration coverage is planned for the new components and their
success/error paths. That coverage does not exercise legacyAuthFlow() or
assert compatibility with its prior behavior.

## Architecture
Two new services (`AuthBroker` and `SessionMint`) share a global mutable
`AuthCache` instance via module-level export. Both services mutate it.

## Code quality
The `validateAndDispatch()` function is 60 lines with three nested
try/catch blocks; each catch swallows a different error class.

## Tests
The existing `legacyAuthFlow()` will get rewritten as part of this work;
no regression test for the prior behavior is planned.

## Performance
Token validation issues 5 sequential API calls to the IDP; they could be
parallelized via Promise.all trivially (calls are independent).

## Architecture (scope smell)
This touches 12 files and introduces 5 new classes (AuthBroker, TokenStore,
SessionMint, AuthCache, RequestPolicy). Worth flagging the complexity check.

questions.question:
D1 — Should the Promise.all IDP parallelization ship in this refactor PR, or as its own follow-up?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor (PLAN.md), Scope Challenge complexity gate.
ELI10: The plan promises "no product behavior change" (PLAN.md:8-9), then also proposes turning 5 sequential calls to the identity provider into 5 parallel ones (PLAN.md:39-41). Parallel calls change which error the user sees when one fails, stop waiting for the others on first failure, and hit the IDP 5x harder at once. That is real behavior, not reorganization. If something breaks after the merge, you will not know whether the refactor or the parallelization did it.
Stakes if we pick wrong: bundle them and a regression in login is un-bisectable; cut it and users keep waiting ~5x longer on token validation than they need to.
Recommendation: A because the speedup is real and cheap, but it deserves its own PR with its own error-semantics tests so the refactor stays a pure structural change.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Defer to an immediate follow-up PR (recommended)
  ✅ Refactor PR stays honest to "no behavior change"; any login regression bisects cleanly to one PR
  ✅ Follow-up PR can carry its own tests for fail-fast ordering, partial-failure and IDP rate limits
  ❌ Users wait one more release cycle for the latency win (human: ~1 day / CC: ~10 min of extra PR overhead)
B) Include in this PR as planned
  ✅ One review, one merge, latency win lands with the refactor
  ✅ AuthBroker is written parallel-first instead of retrofitted later
  ❌ Refactor is no longer behavior-preserving; a 3am login incident has two suspects instead of one
C) Cut parallelization entirely
  ✅ Zero new risk surface in the auth path
  ✅ Nothing to test beyond the refactor itself
  ❌ Leaves a known, trivially fixable ~5x latency on every token validation on the table indefinitely
Net: you are trading one release cycle of latency for a refactor you can actually trust and bisect.

options.label: A) Defer to follow-up PR (recommended)
options.description: Keep this PR structural only. Parallelization ships next as its own PR with fail-fast/partial-failure tests. Recorded as NOT in scope for this plan.

options.label: B) Include in this PR
options.description: Ship Promise.all inside the refactor. Plan's "no behavior change" claim gets amended to name this exception. Performance section will still review the fail-fast semantics.

options.label: C) Cut parallelization
options.description: Drop it from the plan and do not schedule a follow-up. Sequential IDP calls stay as they are.

That is a function, not a class; the author already flagged the boundary as open. TokenStore is never described anywhere, while AuthCache is already "a facade over that same existing adapter, with one backing cache" (PLAN.md:20-21). Two cache-shaped classes over one cache is a duplication smell, but I cannot see TokenStore's code, so that one is medium confidence. Every option keeps the same features, contracts and the D1/D2 answers; this is structure only. The shared-mutable-cache problem (PLAN.md:28-29) is a separate Architecture question and stays pending here.
Stakes if we pick wrong: too many classes and every future auth change touches five files and five test suites; too few and you cram unrelated responsibilities together and get a god-object AuthBroker.
Recommendation: B because RequestPolicy-as-function is a clear win with no downside, while folding TokenStore needs the author to confirm it has no responsibility distinct from AuthCache.

A) Keep all 5 classes as planned
  ✅ Every responsibility has a named home; matches the plan the team already discussed
  ✅ RequestPolicy as a class can grow strategies later without a signature change
  ❌ A one-method stateless class is premature abstraction; five suites for what is one orchestration path
B) 4 parts: RequestPolicy becomes a pure exported function; keep TokenStore (recommended)
  ✅ evaluateRequestPolicy(claims, ctx) is trivially unit-testable with no constructor or mocks
  ✅ Removes one class and its test scaffolding while touching nothing whose role is unclear
  ❌ TokenStore's overlap with AuthCache stays unresolved; plan must define TokenStore's distinct job or this becomes a follow-up
C) 3 parts: RequestPolicy as function AND TokenStore folded into AuthCache
  ✅ One cache facade, one truth about tenant keys and invalidation; least surface for a shared-state bug
  ✅ Fewest files and suites to maintain for a change that claims no behavior difference
  ❌ If TokenStore actually owns something AuthCache does not (e.g. refresh-token persistence), you merge two responsibilities and have to split them again later
Net: B takes the free simplification now and makes the plan author write down what TokenStore is for before deciding its fate.

D4 — How should AuthBroker and SessionMint get their shared AuthCache?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor (PLAN.md), Architecture review (D1–D3 fixed).
ELI10: The plan has both new services import one mutable AuthCache object from a module (PLAN.md:28-29). Anything that imports it can change it, tests share it unless someone remembers to reset it, and you cannot hand a service a fake cache without monkey-patching the module. Passing the cache into each service's constructor from one place at startup keeps a single shared cache in production but makes every dependency visible and every test isolated. The cache itself, its tenant keys and invalidation rules do not change under any option.
Stakes if we pick wrong: with the module export, a test that leaks a cached token into the next test passes locally and hides a tenant-isolation bug; in production, any stray importer can mutate auth state with no owner.
Recommendation: A because it is the Layer 1 answer, costs a constructor parameter per service, and makes the R2 write-ordering fix far easier to place.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Constructor injection from one composition root (recommended)
  ✅ Every test gets a fresh cache or a fake by passing an argument; no shared state between tests
  ✅ Dependency is explicit in the type signature; grep shows exactly who can mutate the cache
  ❌ One more wiring line at startup and a constructor param per service (human: ~1h / CC: ~5 min)
B) Module export behind a getter with resetForTests()
  ✅ Minimal change from the plan; import sites stay the same
  ✅ Tests can reset state between cases
  ❌ Hidden dependency stays hidden; resetForTests() in production code is a smell and easy to forget to call
C) Keep module-level mutable export as proposed
  ✅ Zero extra wiring; shortest path to a working diff
  ✅ No cons beyond those already named in the plan
  ❌ Two writers on an unowned global in the auth path; test isolation depends on discipline, not structure
Net: one constructor parameter buys explicit ownership of auth state and isolated tests.

options.label: A) Constructor injection (recommended)
options.description: AuthBroker and SessionMint take `cache: AuthCache` in their constructors. One AuthCache instance is built at the composition root and passed to both. The module exports the class/factory, not an instance. Same single backing cache in production.

options.label: B) Getter + resetForTests()
options.description: Keep the module-level instance but access it via `getAuthCache()` and add `resetAuthCacheForTests()`. Services keep importing from the module.

options.label: C) Keep as proposed
options.description: Module-level mutable export, imported and mutated directly by both services.

questions.question:
D5 — Can a SessionMint write re-cache a token that was just revoked?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor (PLAN.md), Architecture review (D1–D4 fixed).
ELI10: The plan says the cache does not serialize mutations and that two services both write to it (PLAN.md:19, :29). Picture this: a tenant gets suspended and the invalidation hook clears its entries. A millisecond earlier, SessionMint had finished minting a session for that tenant and is about to write it. Its write lands after the clear. Now a suspended tenant has a valid cached token until it expires. I cannot see the adapter, so this is medium confidence: if invalidation bumps the policy-version part of the key, stale writes are already unreachable and this is a non-issue. The fix, if needed, is small and lives entirely in the new AuthCache facade: track an invalidation epoch per tenant and drop writes that carry an old one.
Stakes if we pick wrong: ignore a real race and a revoked or suspended tenant keeps access for one token lifetime; build the guard when the adapter already covers it and you carry ~40 unnecessary lines plus a test.
Recommendation: A because the guard is cheap, adapter-independent, and makes the facade's safety not depend on an adapter detail nobody has verified; the interleaving test documents the invariant either way.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=3/10, C=n/a (investigation approves no implementation)
Pros / cons:
A) Epoch-guarded writes in the AuthCache facade (recommended)
  ✅ Revocation/suspension always wins over an in-flight mint write, regardless of adapter internals
  ✅ Adapter and its tests stay untouched; guard and interleaving test are ~40 lines in new code (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
  ❌ Slight extra bookkeeping per tenant in the facade; redundant if the adapter already keys invalidations by version
B) Accept as proposed, document the risk
  ✅ Zero extra code in this PR
  ✅ Keeps the facade a pure pass-through as the plan describes
  ❌ A suspended tenant may retain a cached token for one lifetime; nobody will find this in a unit test
C) Investigate the adapter first, remedy stays pending
  ✅ Avoids building a guard the adapter may already provide
  ✅ Bounded: one read of the adapter's invalidation and key code, then this question returns
  ❌ Blocks the plan on a probe; if the race is real you end up doing A anyway, later
Net: ~40 lines in new code versus trusting an unverified adapter detail on the path that decides whether a suspended tenant stays logged in.

options.label: A) Epoch-guarded facade writes (recommended)
options.description: AuthCache keeps a per-tenant invalidation epoch, bumps it on every invalidation hook, and `put()` drops writes carrying a stale epoch. Add an interleaving test: mint-read → invalidate → mint-write must not re-cache. Adapter unchanged.

options.label: B) Accept as proposed
options.description: No guard. Record "post-invalidation write race" as an accepted known risk in the plan.

options.label: C) Investigate adapter first
options.description: Read the adapter's invalidation/key code in the real repo before choosing. R2 remedy stays pending; nothing else changes.

questions.question:
D6 — How should validateAndDispatch() handle the errors it currently swallows?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor (PLAN.md), Code Quality review (D1–D5 fixed).
ELI10: The plan's new orchestration function is 60 lines with three try/catch blocks nested inside each other, and each one quietly eats a different kind of error (PLAN.md:32-33). At 3am, "quietly eats" means the IDP timed out, the user got denied or half-dispatched, and the log says nothing. The user-facing result must stay what it is today; this question is only about making the path explicit: three small steps, one shared error mapper, every failure named in the return type and logged. Anything the code did not anticipate fails closed to a deny instead of vanishing.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a swallowed IDP failure looks identical to a policy deny in production; you cannot tell an outage from a permissions bug, and a partial dispatch after a swallowed error is a security question you cannot answer from logs.
Recommendation: A because three nested catches doing similar work is a DRY violation with a silent-failure bonus, and the split costs minutes with AI while keeping the user outcome identical.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Pros / cons:
A) Three steps + discriminated AuthOutcome + one error mapper (recommended)
  ✅ Every error class has one named outcome; unknown errors are logged and fail closed, never silent
  ✅ Each step is unit-testable alone; the DRY mapper replaces three near-identical catch bodies (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ❌ More small units to read; the return type is a new concept for the team to learn
B) Keep 3 try/catch, log and rethrow typed AuthError
  ✅ Minimal restructuring; errors stop being silent
  ✅ Caller decides the mapping, so behavior stays centralized
  ❌ Still three nested blocks in one 60-line function; still three copies of near-identical catch logic
C) Keep as proposed
  ✅ No extra work in this PR
  ✅ Matches whatever legacy did, if legacy also swallowed
  ❌ Silent failures on the auth path; the plan itself lists this as a code-quality problem
Net: same user result, but you can tell an outage from a deny in the logs and test each step alone.

options.label: A) Split + AuthOutcome + mapper (recommended)
options.description: `validate()` → `RequestPolicy.evaluate()` → `dispatch()`, each returning a discriminated `AuthOutcome`. One `mapAuthError()` for all known error classes; unknown → `error{unknown}`, logged with tenant and request id, fails closed to today's deny response.

options.label: B) Log + rethrow typed AuthError
options.description: Keep the three try/catch blocks; each catch logs and rethrows a typed `AuthError`. Caller maps to the same deny.

options.label: C) Keep as proposed
options.description: 60 lines, three nested swallowing catches.

D7 — How do we prove AuthBroker behaves exactly like legacyAuthFlow() before traffic moves?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor (PLAN.md), Test review (D1–D6 fixed). This is the mandatory regression contract: the question is how to cover, not whether.
ELI10: The plan rewrites the login decision path and says outright that the new tests will not check the old behavior (PLAN.md:23-25, :36-37). Because D2 keeps the old flow alive behind a flag, you can run the old and new code on the same inputs and demand identical answers: same allow/deny, same error response, same cache state. That table of inputs is the contract. Option B pins the old behavior in tests and checks the new code against the same table separately; it catches most drift but not side effects you forgot to list.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a tenant edge case the fixture table misses flips from deny to allow after the flag goes on, and the first signal is a customer.
Recommendation: A because running both paths on one fixture table is the strongest possible parity check, costs minutes with AI, and self-deletes with the legacy code.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10
Pros / cons:
A) Differential parity suite + characterization anchor (recommended)
  ✅ Catches any decision, response or cache-state difference on every fixture, including ones nobody thought to assert individually
  ✅ Doubles as the canary gate: flag flips only when the suite is green (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30 min)
  ❌ Needs a shared fake IDP harness both paths can run against; one more suite to keep green during the window
B) Characterization tests on legacy + independent AuthBroker tests on the same table
  ✅ Simpler harness; each path tested on its own terms
  ✅ Legacy behavior gets pinned before anyone touches it
  ❌ Only asserts what you remembered to list; cache side-effect drift between paths can slip through
Net: the same fixture table either way; A also runs both paths on it and refuses to let them disagree.

options.description: Shared fixture table (12+ cases listed in the grid). Each case runs `legacyAuthFlow()` and `AuthBroker.validateAndDispatch()` against the same fake IDP and a fresh `AuthCache`; assert equal decision, response shape and post-call cache state. Characterization tests pin legacy outputs. Suite gates the flag flip and is deleted with legacy.

Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor (PLAN.md), Test review (D1–D7 fixed).
ELI10: D2 put a switch in front of the login path and D7 proves the two paths agree at the function level. A) Three E2E journeys with fake IDP (recommended)
  ✅ Exercises the real entrypoint, middleware, flag read and response shape for both paths and the flag-failure fallback
  ✅ The same journeys are what you run against the canary tenant before widening the flag (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ❌ Needs an E2E harness with a fake IDP; slower than unit tests, one more thing in CI
B) Integration tests at the routing point only
  ✅ Fast, already carried by D2; no new harness
  ✅ Covers the routing decision itself
  ❌ Blind to anything between the HTTP edge and the routing function; auth flows are exactly where that gap bites
Net: three slow tests versus discovering a middleware-order bug from the canary tenant.
